newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of miners in Bonn, protest at cuts.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of miners in Bonn, protest at cuts.

text.p: Thousands of angry German miners descended on Bonn on Monday to protest against plans to cut coal subsidies, accusing the government of breaking a promise to phase out the aid gradually.
Work in Germany's 18 pits ground to a halt on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) from nine billion by the year 2005.

Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said hundreds of miners would sleep at the party's headquarters ready for protests on Tuesday, when union leaders meet the government to seek a compromise and up to 20,000 miners are expected to protest.
The SPD boycotted talks with the government on planned tax reforms last week in protest at the planned cuts, and said future cooperation would depend on the outcome of the meeting.

Volunteers unloaded truckloads of sleeping bags and blankets and prepared hot food and drinks for the demonstrators, who said they would continue to block entrances to party buildings of the ruling coalition overnight.

The miners' union IG Bergbau says government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 of Germany's 90,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
While miners accept their industry's days are numbered, they argue that a minimum of 6.5 billion marks in subsidies until 2005 is essential to stem spiralling unemployment in mining regions.

"If they don't come to a reasonable agreement we're not giving in. If we don't get what we want we'll stick it out to the bitter end," said miner Dieter Hausmann, 44, who had travelled to Bonn from Moers in the Ruhr valley.

In motorcycle convoys, cars and vans, 3,000 miners came to Bonn, where they blockaded a main road through the government quarter as well as the headquarters of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP).

Miners occupied town halls, pits and highways across Germany's Ruhr industrial heartland and Saar state on the French border. In Saar, miners continued to block a motorway which is the country's main route to Luxembourg.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said the government would stand firm by its "fair and comprehensive" offer. But miners cited a previous promise to maintain higher subsidies for longer and accused Bonn of going back on its word.
"The state should continue to help us and not break its promise. It must stop lying and stop thinking about itself," said miner Dirk Ochmann, 33, clad in helmet and overalls.

"I have three children. If I lose my job how am I going to feed them? If I lose my job now I'll be on the scrap heap," Hausmann said outside the offices of the pro-market FDP, the driving force behind the cuts.
"The whole region lives from coal mining. If we go to the free market we'll have 30 percent unemployment."

Miners, many clad in bright orange overalls and hard hats sealed entrances to the FDP party headquarters with chains, forcing it to move its weekly leadership meeting to parliament buildings. The protesters said they would stay there all night.
Nearby, pit workers revving motorbike engines, honking horns and blowing whistles blocked a junction on the main road through the government quarter, forcing traffic to be diverted.
Government officials called the blockades unnecessary.

"I understand that miners are afraid of losing their jobs. (But) no one has done more for the miners in Saar and Ruhr than Helmut Kohl and the CDU," said CDU general secretary Peter Hintze, whose office was picketed by miners.
The chief targets of the miners' wrath, Kohl's junior coalition partners in the FDP, were less conciliatory.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle blamed the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) for high unemployment in the key coal mining states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Saar, which the SPD rules, and for failing to restructure industry there. ($ = 1.707 German Marks)
